newsitem.title: USA: Texas near Iran, Iraq in execution rate - Amnesty.
newsitem.headline: Texas near Iran, Iraq in execution rate - Amnesty.

text.p: Texas is executing criminals at such a pace that it is catching up with Iran, Iraq and Saudi Arabia, according to the human rights group Amnesty International.

The state had its eighth execution in the month of May (on) Thursday when it gave a lethal injection to Robert Madden, 33, for the 1985 robbery and murder of a man and his son. Already, 16 people have been executed in Texas this year, and another 10 are scheduled to die in June.
"The state of Texas comes perilously close to matching Iran, Iraq and Saudi Arabia in their astoundingly high rates of execution," Amnesty International said in a statement this week.
"Only a few countries, including Iran, Iraq and Saudi Arabia, execute six or more persons every month," it said.

The three countries have justice systems based on Islamic principles that say criminals should be treated harshly. In Texas, tough justice is a legacy of the state's frontier days, said Andy Kahan, director of crime victim programmes for Houston.

"The spirit of invoking frontier justice has carried on down throughout the decades for the people who live here," he told Reuters on Friday. "If you take the risk, you suffer the consequences (of crime)."

But Amnesty International USA executive director William Schulz called Texas' policies self-defeating. "The residents of Texas, and indeed all Americans, need to stop and look at what we are doing. Amnesty International understands the constant concern about crime and violence in our society; however, the death penalty only foments that violence," he said.
"When murder by the state is officially condoned, we are that much further away from teaching a general respect for life," Schulz said.
Kahan described execution as "punishment plain and simple for the worst crime one human being can inflict on another."
Besides, he said, "when you compare the amount of people executed to the amount murdered every year in this country, the figure is so minuscule it's not worth discussing."

Since the U.S. Supreme Court reinstated capital punishment in 1976, 386 people have been executed in the United States, 123 of them in Texas. Last year, 24,000 people were murdered in the country, Kahan said.
Kahan said he was unconcerned that Texas was being compared to Iran and Iraq, two countries many Americans do not view favourably. "I think we should be proud we uphold our laws," he said.
China, which executes scores of people every month, remains far and away the world's leader in capital punishment, Amnesty International said.
